hypothesis: Enabling CTS sink clustering with a larger max diameter (200um instead of 100um) and larger cluster size (40 instead of 30) reduces clock tree buffer count and clock net routing demand, lowering global-route overflow while also shortening clock insertion delay variance so propagated-clock setup slack improves on all circuits — a CTS-stage (C1) probe independent of the partitioner.
analysis: The hypothesis failed: all three cases show negative scores and worse WNS/TNS (dWNS −3.3% to −3.6%), with overflow still ~130–151, so larger sink clustering did not reduce buffer/routing demand or improve setup slack. The mechanism likely backfired—bigger clusters (40, 200µm) increase skew and insertion-delay spread rather than shorten it, hurting propagated-clock setup. Next step: sweep intermediate diameters (120–150µm) and cluster sizes (32–36) per case, and check clock skew/insertion-delay variance directly at C1 to confirm whether the clustering granularity is the true driver before retesting.
